article_sentences: ITANAGAR: Arunachal Pradesh Rural Development and Panchayati Raj Minister Ojing Tasing on Wednesday said the proposed Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) is important for India's water security and national security, but stressed that the interests and well-being of people affected by the project must be protected through dialogue and consultation.

Tasing, who represents Pangin Assembly constituency in Siang district, said India cannot ignore the large-scale infrastructure development being undertaken by China upstream of the Siang, which is known as the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet and enters India as the Siang before becoming the Brahmaputra.
"The SUMP carries profound significance for India's water security and national security.

At a time when China is undertaking massive infrastructure development upstream, India must remain prepared to safeguard its strategic interests and ensure that our water resources can never become an instrument of pressure against our nation," he said.
The minister, however, said national interest and the welfare of local communities should not be seen as competing objectives.
He stressed that while the country must prepare for strategic challenges, the rights and interests of people living in the project area also have to be given due importance.
"National interest and the welfare of our people must move forward together.
As we secure the nation's future, it is equally our solemn responsibility to protect the rights, interests and well-being of every citizen and community affected by the project," Tasing said.

stories.title: CPI(M) protests over flood relief; protesters detained in Guwahati

article_sentences: GUWAHATI: The Assam State Committee of the CPI(M) on Wednesday organised a massive protest in Guwahati under the banner of "March to Dispur", demanding immediate relief and rehabilitation for flood-affected people in Upper Assam and a judicial inquiry into the causes of the devastating floods.

The protesters also demanded that the Upper Assam floods be declared a "calamity of severe nature", the formation of a North East Flood Management Authority, recognition of floods and erosion in Assam as a national problem, and immediate steps to control the rising prices of essential commodities.
They further sought the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
The programme was scheduled to begin with the gathering of protesters at Volvo Point near Ulubari, followed by a march towards Dispur.
Thousands of people from different parts of Assam reportedly arrived in Guwahati to participate in the programme.
However, the police and civil administration imposed restrictions on the assembly and movement of protesters, with heavy barricading at various entry points to the city.
Several protesters were intercepted at different locations and taken to the Chachal protest ground for detention.
At Guwahati Railway Station, several thousand protesters reportedly broke through police barricades and marched towards Volvo Point.
Some were subsequently intercepted and detained at Chachal.
The CPI(M) claimed that more than 2,000 protesters were detained, while many others could not participate in the programme due to the heavy police deployment and restrictions.

Among those detained were CPI(M) Assam State Secretary Suprakash Talukdar, Central Committee member Isfaqur Rahman, veteran leader Deben Bhattacharya and State Secretariat members Manoranjan Talukdar, Ajit Das, Tiken Das, along with several other party leaders and activists.
Despite the restrictions, the CPI(M) submitted its memorandum addressed to the Chief Minister at the Chachal protest ground through police officials.

stories.title: Gomti swells, flood-like conditions hit Lucknow; relief operations intensified
stories.summary: Gomti swells, flood-like conditions hit Lucknow; relief operations intensified
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Flood-like conditions spread across parts of southern Lucknow on Wednesday as the rising water level of the Gomti river inundated roads and affected several residential areas, including parts of Gomti Nagar Extension.
Waterlogging was reported around Phoenix Palassio mall, Ekana Stadium and the service lanes of Shaheed Path, raising concerns in an area known for its wide roads and recent high-end development.
Parts of Gomti Nagar Extension were also affected, adding to waterlogging already reported in northern and western parts of the city and several older localities over the past few days.
The Lucknow Municipal Corporation said relief and rescue operations had been intensified in affected areas.
These include Saitha in Zone 6 and Loharamau, Faizullaganj, Daud Nagar and Millat Nagar in Zone 3.
Residents in the affected areas reported difficult travelling conditions.

Sachin Sahay, a resident of a high-rise in Sector 7 of Gomti Nagar Extension, said his car nearly went underwater while he was travelling from Rishita Manhattan towards Ansal around 8:15 pm on Wednesday.
“I was going from Rishita Manhattan to Ansal around 8:15 pm when, just after passing the side of Palassio mall, the wheels of my car went nearly underwater.
I somehow managed to reach Shaheed Path.
I was worried that the car might break down and I would have to get my family out into knee-deep water,” he said.
Videos shared on social media showed waterlogging around Gomti Nagar, Shaheed Path, Ekana Stadium and Phoenix Palassio, with water, including drain overflow, accumulating on roads and access routes.
The flooding also triggered a political confrontation.

stories.title: Tamil Nadu CM Vijay claimed ownership over 50 cents of poromboke land in Kodaikanal, alleges election petitioner before Madras High Court

reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay has claimed ownership over 50 cents of government poromboke land at Vilpatti village in Kodaikanal, falsely declared a property sold by him for ₹35 crore at Padi in Chennai as his property worth ₹7 crore and wrongly termed his Neelangarai bungalow as inherited property, an election petitioner has claimed before the Madras High Court.
However, Mr Vijay said the allegations against him were baseless and the petition must be dismissed.

In the petition pending before Justice V. Lakshminarayanan, S. Dinesh, a voter from Perambur constituency, insisted the election of the Chief Minister must be declared null and void for “wilful and deliberate” suppression, misrepresentation and false declarations with respect to many of the immovable properties referred to in his 2026 election affidavit.
According to the petitioner’s counsel V.R. Shanmuganathan, Mr. Vijay had claimed to have purchased the Vilpatti agricultural land for a consideration of ₹30,000 in 1997.
Mr Vijay had also said, the present market value of that property was around ₹20 lakh.
However, an examination of the village ‘A’ register revealed the property was actually a government poromboke land, the counsel claimed.
Similarly, the Chief Minister had declared to have purchased a non agricultural land measuring 33,955 square feet at Porur in Chennai for a consideration of ₹9.13 crore in 2010.
However, examination of registration department documents revealed that he had purchased only 20,773 square feet for ₹7.5 crore.
There was no explanation for excess declaration of the extent of the land as well as the sale amount, the petitioner alleged.

He went on to state that Mr. Vijay had declared to be owning a ₹7 crore worth 11,854 sq.ft commercial building at Padi in Chennai and claimed to have purchased it for a consideration of ₹1.95 crore in 2009 besides spending ₹3.9 crore on construction.
However, he had sold the commercial building with a constructed area of 23,460 sq.ft for a consideration of ₹35 crore on February 12, 2026, the petitioner claimed.

Further, the court was told he had not purchased the commercial property in 2009 as it had been declared in the election affidavit and instead received it in exchange for his Korattur property from Tamil Nadu Housing Board.

stories.headline: India exposes Pak doublespeak at UN, says world has not forgotten 9/11, 26/11 and Pahalgam attacks
stories.title: India exposes Pak doublespeak at UN, says world has not forgotten 9/11, 26/11 and Pahalgam attacks
stories.summary: United Nations, Oct 08: Exposing Pakistan’s doublespeak on terrorism at the UN, India has called out Islamabad’s efforts to gloss over its state support for terror by announcing rewards for JeM chief Masood Azahar, underlining that the world has not forgotten 9/11, 26/11 and Pahalgam attacks. India on Wednesday exercised its Right of Reply in response to the Pakistan representative’s statement in the Sixth Committee of the UN General Assembly on the Agenda Item: Measures to Eliminate International Terrorism. “Pakistan speaks of combating terrorism while seeking to obscure the very question that this committee must confront: What happens when terrorists are financed, facilitated, trained, sheltered, or supported from the territory of a state?” First Secretary in the Permanent Mission of India to the UN Raghoo Puri said. He said India has been consistent on this question, underscoring that terrorism cannot be defeated by declarations and instead requires action against its perpetrators, organisers, financiers, and sponsors. “For years, Pakistan has presented itself as a frontline state in combating terrorism and as a victim while masking the fact that the Frankensteins the Pakistani state has created and lost control over have moved from wreaking havoc in neighbouring countries to doing the same in Pakistan,” Puri said. Calling out Pakistan’s doublespeak on terrorism, Puri said the country “glosses over its state support for terrorism by announcing enhanced rewards for apprehending UN-listed head of Jaish-e-Mohammed terrorist and mastermind of several attacks against my country, Masood Azhar.” He said the world is aware of Pakistan's financial support to terrorism. “Yet, we also remember that just a few months ago, Pakistani representatives used this forum to call the Jaish-e-Mohammed a defunct organisation. The world has seen the script play earlier, and we are clear-eyed that this time also it is going to be no different,” he said. Puri said that when the media can reach Azhar and get confirmation from him about the success of Operation Sindoor, "surely the Pakistani state knows his whereabouts”. In May last year, India had launched Operation Sindoor targeting terror infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir in retaliation for the dastardly April 22 terror attack in Pahalgam in Jammu and Kashmir perpetrated by The Resistance Front, a proxy of Pakistan-based terror group Lashkar-e-Taiba, in which 26 civilians, mostly tourists were killed. Earlier this month, India had dismissed as “gimmicks” Pakistan’s fresh announcement of a bounty of seven million rupees on Azhar, demanding that Islamabad take “concrete action” to combat terrorism. India has for years accused Pakistan of sheltering Azhar, while Pakistan has maintained that he fled to Afghanistan – a claim rejected by Afghanistan’s Taliban government. For the last few years, Islamabad has claimed that the JeM founder has been operating from Afghanistan. However, the Taliban regime dismissed Pakistan’s repeated claims, with a senior Afghan Foreign Ministry official saying he is not in the country. Islamabad’s fresh announcement on the reward for information on Azhar came as it faces pressure from the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) to crack down on terror groups and their leadership. The Paris-based global watchdog is set to review Pakistan’s anti-terrorism efforts at its upcoming plenary. Pakistan was placed under the FATF grey list between 2018 and 2022 for its systemic deficiencies in anti-money laundering and its failure to counter-terror financing. Puri also recalled a recent statement by Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, daughter of former Pakistan prime minister Nawaz Sharif, who had said,“The unfortunate thing is that the threat [Punjab] faces comes less from my neighbouring countries and more from my neighbouring provinces.” Exposing this “dark secret”, Puri said, “You cannot run with the hares and hunt with the hounds. Reality never works like that.” “When terrorist groups are allowed to operate under state political power, international commitments become meaningless and when perpetrators are provided safe havens, the victims of terrorism are denied justice,” he said. “The world has not forgotten 9/11 and where its perpetrators, including Osama bin Laden, were caught. The world has not forgotten 26/11. The world has not forgotten Pahalgam,” Puri said, adding that the list, “unfortunately”, is painfully long. “The victims in Pahalgam were not asked about their political orientation, they were asked about their religion. It is therefore deeply ironic that Pakistan speaks of combating religious hatred while allowing the conditions that enable it to persist and thrive, especially by fomenting cross-border terrorism,” he said. “Pakistan continues with its narrative building, misinformation, and disinformation. If bombed-out airfields and cratered runways look like victory to Pakistan, they are of course welcome to enjoy it," Puri said. "Any regime against terrorism to be effective must do two things: assign responsibility and ensure accountability. India will defend its people, and continued terrorism against India will have consequences,” he added. In another Right of Reply, Puri said India rejected Pakistan’s “circular economy” of words and narratives. “If this much effort had actually been made in countering terrorism rather than narrative building, misinformation, and disinformation, the world would have been a better place. But nothing more can be expected from a Form 47 government,” he said, referring to a term used to describe allegations of rigging and manipulation in Pakistan’s 2024 general elections.

stories.headline: The Gateway Paradox
stories.title: The Gateway Paradox
stories.summary: TECHNOLOGY & NATIONAL SECURITY Kashmir knows what it is to lose a connection by order. India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, according to Access Now, and in Jammu and Kashmir the authorities went after VPN users under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, penalising roughly 800 people. Satellite broadband looks like the answer. A dish on a rooftop in a high-altitude village needs no local tower and no fibre run. In early September, the Digital Communications Commission approved a spectrum framework that moves Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio’s satellite venture closer to commercial launch. But a network with no towers still has a throat. Every one of these services must land its traffic at a gateway on Indian soil, and whoever controls the gateway controls the switch. What the framework approves, and what it does not According to MediaNama, the commission cleared TRAI’s recommendations on 3 September. Spectrum would be assigned for five years, with a possible two-year extension, at 5 per cent of adjusted gross revenue. Operators serving rural and remote areas may get a 4 per cent rate. The Department of Telecommunications rejected a proposed Rs 500 annual levy on urban subscribers. Three steps remain: Union Cabinet approval, formal spectrum assignment, and security clearance from the Ministry of Home Affairs. The draft spectrum rules reported in June go further. They require government approval before consumer services launch, and they require authorisation to connect a satellite network to public telecom infrastructure. Starlink’s own plans show where the weight sits. MediaNama reports about 20 earth stations across Noida, Chennai and Navi Mumbai, a capacity of up to 2 million users, and a terminal costing around Rs 33,000. Two million connections would run through a few facilities in three cities. A shutdown that moves from the tower to the gateway Today, a suspension order in Kashmir lands on telecom operators and their local infrastructure, district by district. It is blunt, and it is visible. Satellite links change the mechanics. If traffic for a whole footprint passes through a handful of gateways, one lawful order to one facility could darken a large area at once. “The dish on the roof is hard to cut. The gateway in Noida is easy to switch off.” That is my inference, and it has limits. The licence conditions that would govern gateway shutdowns are not public, and I could not verify whether they allow targeted, area-by-area suspension. What is public is the direction. MediaNama reported in June that security agencies under the Home Ministry had frozen Starlink’s final clearances and wanted monitoring systems inside India and regular reporting to law enforcement. Starlink disputed the freeze and called its talks with the government “active and productive”. The design has a security logic. A gateway on Indian soil is the only place where Delhi can enforce anything against a foreign operator. It is also the place where a promise of shutdown-proof connectivity gets tested. The beam does not read maps MediaNama also reports that agencies are examining signal spillover near the borders. A satellite footprint over the Valley does not stop at the Line of Control. The same constellation that serves Gurez serves territory on the other side. Terminals add a second worry. The Indian Army recovered what it described as a Starlink device with weapons in Manipur in December 2024, per MediaNama, and terminals worked in Iran during that country’s conflict without proper licensing. A Rs 33,000 terminal fits in a rucksack. The state’s likely response is tighter control at the two points it can reach: the gateway and the terminal registry. Both are felt first by the legitimate user in a remote district. The smuggler who skips the registry still depends on a gateway that will carry the traffic, which is why the location of that gateway matters so much to security agencies. The steelman Keeping gateways in India is better than the alternative. A foreign operator running a network over Indian territory with no domestic control point would be a sovereignty problem of a different kind, and the Iran episode shows why agencies worry. Satellite links also survive physical damage that would take a tower or a cable offline, and that has real value in a region of floods and snowfall. So the argument is narrower. Resilience and control are being sold as one product, and they are two. The first protects users from accidents. The second protects the state from users, and the licence conditions will decide which one dominates. Bottom Line Satellite broadband will make India’s border regions harder to cut off by accident. It will also make them easier to switch off on purpose, from a few buildings in Noida, Chennai and Navi Mumbai. Before the Cabinet signs off, Delhi should publish the conditions under which a gateway can be ordered dark, and say who reviews that order. Kashmir has lived with the unpublished version for long enough. (The Author studies Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence at Rutgers University, New Jersey, USA. He is interested in emerging technologies and innovation, and can be reached on LinkedIn at @arssh-kumar14)

stories.headline: J&K GCC Summit 2026: The Arithmetic of a Capability Centre
stories.title: J&K GCC Summit 2026: The Arithmetic of a Capability Centre
stories.summary: Ask the chief financial officer of a Global Capability Centre what it costs to run. The answer begins with people. Salaries, pension, gratuity, power subsidy and social benefits take the largest share of UT's annual budget. That simple fact should shape how Jammu and Kashmir competes for the sector. And that simple fact is what the J&K Government is going to position at the J&K GCC Summit 2026, being organized by the Government of J&K and IIM Jammu. If a capability centre is a ten-year commitment to recurring cost, the location decision turns on what the centre will cost to run in its fifth and eighth years, discounted to today. The one-time cost of setting up is a minor line in that calculation. We have 55 investors from the world's leading Fortune 500 GCC and GCC- enabling companies and India's leading multinationals descending at IIM Jammu on 9-10 October for the Summit. And each one of them perhaps already knows that a capital subsidy, however generous, only addresses the smallest part of the problem. A subsidy is easy to announce, and it makes good PR. But what moves a location decision is sustained relief on recurring cost. That means employment- linked support for each professional hired and retained, a defined share of payroll cost reimbursed for a limited period, lease rental assistance, electricity tariff subsidy, stamp duty relief on leases and a grant for each candidate trained and placed. Outcome-linked support also has a fiscal property that capital subsidies lack. Its cost rises only when jobs rise. The exposure of the exchequer is therefore bounded by success and can be budgeted year by year against verified employment. A capital subsidy is paid at the start, whatever happens afterwards. Recovering it from a nucleus that underperforms is slow and uncertain. Retention is the second variable. Here Jammu and Kashmir holds a structural advantage. Consider an illustrative centre of 500 professionals. At an annual attrition rate of 20 per cent it must replace 100 people every year. At 10 per cent it replaces 50. Over a decade, the difference is 500 replacements, equivalent to rebuilding the entire centre once over. Each replacement carries the cost of recruitment, training and months of reduced productivity. Professionals who work in Jammu and Kashmir are, for the most part, working where their families live. The pull of a marginally better offer across town, which drives much of the churn in metropolitan clusters, operates with far less force here. Add office, talent and utility costs well below metropolitan levels, and the Union Territory has a cost position that rests on its own fundamentals. The competition is real. At least eight States have notified dedicated GCC policies, from Karnataka, which moved first, to Haryana in May 2026. Tamil Nadu addresses the sector through a dedicated framework and Andhra Pradesh through its IT policy. Their incentive menus vary widely. So do the thresholds at which benefits begin. A Union Territory without an existing GCC base cannot borrow a threshold designed for a mature cluster. It must set thresholds that a first entrant can realistically meet. J&K's GCC Policy has been drafted and will be showcased to the prospective GCC multinationals that are attending the J&K GCC Summit. These multinationals will benchmark J&K against the above expected benefits. Be that as it may, we should assess support for the sector in J&K against five rules. First, pay for outcomes. Support from the J&k Government should be attached to jobs created and sustained, payroll actually paid and candidates actually placed, each verified against EPFO and ESIC records, the exchequer may pay for delivery and only after it. Second, setting a horizon. Every incentive should reduce over time and end on a known date, so that a centre's economics is tested on its own profitability rather than continuing purely because of support. Third, avoid paying twice. A Union Territory instrument should fill the gaps left by Central and Union Territory schemes already in force for industry and skilling, chiefly on operating and lease cost and not vice versa. Fourth, weigh the return. At an illustrative average salary of R10 lakh a year, a centre of 500 professionals pays R50 crore in salaries every year, much of it spent locally. It pays stamp duty on its leases. Its local spending and the consumption of its employees generate GST. It supports a comparable number of indirect jobs in facilities, transport and hospitality. For a Union Territory working to strengthen its own revenue base, a sector whose spending stays local is fiscally attractive. Fifth, publish the ledger. The incentives paid, and the jobs verified against them should be disclosed every year. Transparency is the cheapest way to sustain public confidence in industrial incentives. But then, the caveat is that no incentive can compensate for an unclear approval timeline, a building that is yet to be built or a talent pipeline that falls short of an employer's requirement. And that is where the J&K Government is ensuring that investors, and not just from the GCC ecosystem, are provided clear approval timelines, assessed and industry-ready talent pool and infrastructure that is plug- and-play ready than bare land. As I mentioned earlier, the J&K GCC Summit 2026 at IIM Jammu on 9 and 10 October gives the Union Territory a rare opportunity to hear from operators what actually can work for us to be considered as the emerging destination for GCCs. Join the conversation and give us your inputs on what may work. Well, this is a first step, and we hope one that goes a million miles. (The writer is Additional Chief Secretary, Finance Department, Government of Jammu and Kashmir)

article_sentences: The Supreme Court today called for suggestions on the creation of a dedicated corpus for providing financial assistance to people suffering from Spinal Muscular Atrophy, a rare genetic disorder.
A bench of CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana was dealing with a suo motu case taken up over lack of adequate and systematic treatment for SMA patients.
Senior Advocate Aparajita Singh (appointed as Amicus Curiae) and ASG Anil Kaushik appeared.

The case is an offshoot of the proceedings related to comedian Samay Raina and others, who were accused by M/s Cure SMA Foundation of making insensitive jokes about Persons with Disabilities (including those suffering from SMA).
After certain directions by the Court, the comedians apologized and took steps for making amends.
Thereafter, the proceedings were closed and the Court took up the present suo motu case to address the issue of systematic issues in treatment of SMA.
During today's hearing, the CJI asked the Union and the Amicus to suggest a proposal for establishing a dedicated corpus.
The judge expressed that the proposed corpus can include CSR contributions and government grants, but it should be permanent and not incidental in nature.
"it should not depend on the incidental circumstance that today CSR has come or upon persuasion, the government has released the grant...that should not be the case.
But what is the regular channel...a permanent system...kind of an automated nudge to contribution", CJI said.
The judge underlined that the focus should be more towards optimal utilization of the fund, instead of generating the fund.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Union Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, and Home Minister Amit Shah, along with the UP and Assam Chief Ministers, extended greetings to the air warriors on Indian Air Force Day, thanking them for serving the nation with dedication and praising their courage.
In a video posted on X, PM said, "India is proud of our Air Warriors.
On Air Force Day, we salute their courage and commitment to protect our skies!"
He congratulated all the air warriors and their families who have served the country.
“Things in the sky are always unpredictable; it is no surprise that by showcasing its power in the sky, the IAF has drawn the attention of every citizen and given a sense of security, " he said.
Union Home Minister Amit Shah took to social media and said, "Salutations to the Warriors of Our Skies on the glorious occasion of Indian Air Force Day."
"A legion of real-life brave hearts whose saga of invincible valour, laser-sharp precision and devastating striking capabilities is testified by the Earth and satellites in faraway space.
Their patriotism and professionalism will continue to inspire generations long after the daydreams of India's enemies cease to exist.
I bow to the martyrs who laid down their lives for the nation," he added.

The Uttar Pradesh and Assam Chief Ministers said "From the infinite heights of the sky to the nation's borders, the Indian Air Force, the embodiment of valour, strength, and resolve, is the pride of us all." They saluted the sacrifice and unwavering commitment of the air warriors.

Air Chief Marshal A P Singh said the Indian Air Force has, on the one hand, demonstrated its speed and strike power to the world during combat operations and, on the other, it has consistently promoted ‘Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam’ by providing humanitarian aid globally.

stories.headline: Nana Patekar passes away, leaves behind an iconic cinematic legacy
stories.title: Nana Patekar passes away, leaves behind an iconic cinematic legacy
stories.summary: Mumbai, Oct 8 : Veteran actor Nana Patekar, one of Indian cinema's most powerful and distinctive performers, passed away at the age of 75 on Thursday, October 8, 2026. Born Vishwanath Patekar on January 1, 1951, in Murud-Janjira, Maharashtra, Nana Patekar went on to become one of the most respected actors in Hindi and Marathi cinema. The legendary actor was known for his intense screen presence, distinctive voice, powerpack dialogue delivery and ability to bring raw emotional depth to his characters, Nana Patekar enjoyed a career spanning nearly five decades with his association with acting beginning long before his film career. For the uninitiated, the actor studied at the Sir J.J. School of Art in Mumbai and was actively involved in theatre. He made his Hindi film debut with Gaman in 1978. His early years saw him moving between Hindi and Marathi cinema, with his Marathi film debut coming with Sinhasan in 1979. He then appeared in Marathi films including Bhalu, Raghu Maina and Savitri. Nana Patekar had already appeared in many films, but his career gained significant momentum with N. Chandra's Ankush in 1986. The film saw him portraying a character rooted in the struggles and frustrations of ordinary people. He then appeared in films such as Pratighaat, Mohre, Andhaa Yudh and Salaam Bombay! and eventually went on to be known for portraying layered characters rather than conventional romantic heroes. One of the defining milestones of Nana Patekar's career came with Vidhu Vinod Chopra's Parinda in 1989. His portrayal of the ruthless crime boss Anna earned him the National Film Award for Best Supporting Actor. Nana Patekar continued to take on dramatically challenging roles through the 1990s with movies like Agni Sakshi, Khamoshi: The Musical, Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman, Angaar, Tirangaa, Ghulam-E-Mustafa, Yeshwant and Kohram. In 2004, Nana Patekar delivered another career-defining performance in Ab Tak Chhappan, directed by Shimit Amin. He played Sadhu Agashe, a Mumbai Police encounter specialist, in a performance that combined restraint with his trademark intensity. His work in Prakash Jha's Apaharan in 2005 earned him a lot of applause and awards. He also appeared in films including Taxi No. 9211, Welcome, Raajneeti, The Attacks of 26/11 and Kaala. While the legendary actor was largely associated with intense dramatic roles, his performance as Uday Shetty in Welcome 2007 introduced audiences to another side of the actor. His chemistry with Anil Kapoor and his comic timing turned Uday Shetty into one of the most memorable characters in mainstream Hindi comedy. Despite becoming a major name in Hindi cinema, Nana Patekar never forgot his Maharashtrian roots and always retained a strong connection with Marathi theatre and cinema. His Marathi filmography includes Sinhasan, Bhalu, Raghu Maina, Savitri, Pak Pak Pakaak, Deool, Natsamrat, Aapla Manus and Dr. Prakash Baba Amte: The Real Hero, among others. His performance in Natsamrat in 2016), based on V. V. Shirwadkar's celebrated Marathi play, became one of the most significant performances of his later career. He essayed the character of Ganpat Belwalkar, a retired stage actor who struggles with ageing, family relationships and the loss of his place in society, Nana brought his theatrical background to the forefront. Another important Marathi performance came in Dr. Prakash Baba Amte: The Real Hero, for which he won many awards and a lot of appreciation. For the uninitiated, Nana Patekar also explored filmmaking behind the camera. He made his directorial debut with Prahaar: The Final Attack in 1991, a film centred on the Indian Army and the life of a highly disciplined commando. In 2013, he was honoured with the Padma Shri, India's fourth-highest civilian award, for his contribution to the arts and cinema. His other Marathi movies include Bhalu, Raghu Maina, Savitri, Maaficha Sakshidar, Pak Pak Pakaak, Deool, Yashwantrao Chavan – Bakhar Eka Vaadalaachi, , Aapla Manus and Ole Aale. Nana Patekar, despite being a legend on the silver screen, always managed to keep his personal life away from the media glare. The actor married actress Neelakanti Patekar in 1978, and had two sons, Durvasa and Malhar. Reportedly their elder son, Durvasa, tragically passed away at around two-and-a-half years of age due to illness. Their younger son, Malhar Patekar, is associated with working behind the camera in films and has largely maintained a low profile. Beyond cinema, the legendary star was also associated with social initiatives, particularly work supporting farmers and families affected by drought in Maharashtra. The veteran actor’s demise has sent shockwaves across the film industry and left his fans deeply saddened. Nana Patekar passed away at the age of 75 on October 8, after reportedly suffering a severe cardiac arrest at his residence in Dona Paula, Goa, in the early hours of Thursday. He was found unconscious and was subsequently rushed to Manipal Hospital, where doctors attempted to revive him through continuous CPR. However, their efforts were unsuccessful, and he was declared dead. –IANS
